title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Offshore | Dye Penetrant (US)
description: On-site liquid penetrant testing for Gulf of Mexico platforms and yards: stainless, duplex and aluminum welds with controlled materials. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Offshore Platforms and Yards in the United States
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT) finds surface-breaking cracks and porosity on nonmagnetic offshore metals: stainless and duplex piping, chemical injection and instrument tubing, aluminum helidecks and accommodation structure, and weld repairs where magnetizing is not practical. Atlantis mobilizes qualified technicians to Gulf of Mexico platforms, supply bases and fabrication yards in the United States. To scope a job, request a PT inspection quote and include your weld list and materials.

Why offshore programs need penetrant testing

Magnetic particle testing is the quick choice for the carbon steel that dominates platform structure, but a lot of offshore equipment is not carbon steel. Corrosion-resistant alloys are used where seawater, produced fluids and chlorides punish ordinary steel: 316L and duplex stainless piping, super duplex flowlines and manifolds, nickel-alloy cladding, titanium and copper-nickel seawater systems, and aluminum for helidecks and lightweight modules. None of these can be examined by MT. Penetrant testing works on all of them, which makes it the standard surface method for offshore alloy welds and repairs. For structural carbon steel the better tool is magnetic particle testing for offshore, and for wall thickness it is ultrasonic testing for offshore.

Regulations and codes

The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement regulates Gulf of Mexico Outer Continental Shelf operations under 30 CFR Part 250, and operators run inspection through their safety and environmental management systems. API RP 2A and the API structural integrity management practice guide platform structures, AWS D1.1 covers structural welds, ASME B31.3 covers topsides piping and ASME Section VIII covers pressure vessels. Penetrant testing is performed per ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as the common practice standard. Acceptance comes from the code or operator specification. Atlantis reports; the operator's inspector accepts or rejects.

Offshore components where PT is the right method

  • Stainless and duplex process piping and instrument tubing: welds on small-bore lines, chemical injection skids, hydraulic control lines and sample systems.
  • Super duplex and nickel-alloy flowline spools and manifolds: weld surfaces and repairs before hydrotest, with strict control of halogen and sulfur in the penetrant materials.
  • Aluminum helidecks and modules: weld and fitting cracks in deck extrusions, which can start at stress concentrations from vibration and landing loads.
  • Heat exchanger and cooler tube-sheet welds in copper-nickel or titanium seawater systems.
  • Weld repairs and ground-out areas on any metal, to confirm a flaw is gone before welding and the repair is sound afterward.
  • Machined and sealing surfaces such as flange faces, valve bodies and wellhead components at supply bases and shops, where a crack-like flaw could leak.

Penetrant chemistry and corrosion-resistant alloys

Corrosion-resistant alloys are exactly where penetrant chemistry matters. Chlorides and other halogens, and sulfur, in penetrant, cleaner and developer can attack stainless steel and nickel alloys, especially when the part later sees heat or stress. Article 6 requires controlled halogen and sulfur content for materials used on these alloys, so the penetrant system is chosen for low-contaminant composition and the batch certification is retained. We list the materials and lot numbers in the report so your quality file is complete.

Marine air adds its own chloride load. A weld that sat on a deck in salt air has a film of salt on it, which must be cleaned off before penetrant goes on, because salt crystals plug crack mouths and give false indications. Removal uses the cleaner the procedure names and fresh water where allowed, followed by full drying. After testing, penetrant residue is cleaned so it does not interfere with coatings or enter piping that carries injected chemicals.

How the examination is done in a marine environment

Penetrant steps and offshore adjustments
StepStandard practiceOffshore adjustment
PrecleaningRemove paint, scale, oilAlso remove salt film and marine growth
DryingEvaporate cleaner fullyAllow extra time in humid air
Penetrant applicationApply and dwell per procedureShelter from wind, spray and rain
Excess removalWipe, avoid floodingUse clean lint-free cloths; no seawater
DeveloperThin, even coatApply promptly; wind can leave streaks
ExaminationAdequate white or black lightUse a tent for darkness or shade

Temperature and wetness set the limits. Penetrant techniques are qualified for a surface temperature range, and a Gulf summer deck in direct sun can exceed it, while a winter deck in a norther can fall below it. The procedure covers this by shading or waiting for the right conditions, or by qualification at the actual temperature. Wet or damp surfaces are not tested, since water blocks the penetrant from entering flaws.

Reading indications on corroded and welded surfaces

A real crack bleeds out as a sharp, continuous or stepped line that widens slowly as penetrant is drawn from it. Porosity gives round, scattered dots. A rough or corroded surface holds penetrant and creates diffuse bleed-out that is easy to mistake for a flaw, so doubtful areas are recleaned, retested and sometimes lightly dressed first. The technician records every relevant indication with its length and location and photographs it with a scale. Indications judged nonrelevant, such as bleed at a geometric corner or a surface scratch, are listed and explained, not dropped silently.

Small-bore tubing, control lines and skids

A large share of offshore welds are small. Chemical injection, hydraulic and instrument lines are thin-wall stainless or duplex tubing joined by socket and butt welds, often in tight racks where the technician has limited room. Penetrant testing is the practical surface method there because a probe or yoke will not fit. The technician applies penetrant with a brush or aerosol, controls the wipe carefully to avoid flushing shallow flaws from a narrow weld, and uses an inspection mirror or a direct line of sight to read the developed weld. Tubing on a skid at a yard is far easier to reach than the same tubing installed on a crowded deck, so many operators schedule PT during fabrication, before load-out.

Documentation closes the loop. Each tubing weld or repair receives an identification that matches the weld list, and the report states which joints were examined, which were inaccessible, and which were deferred for a later window. Joints that could not be reached are listed as not examined rather than omitted, so the operator knows the true coverage of the campaign and can plan a return visit.

Weld repairs and crack removal

Whenever a crack is found and removed by grinding, penetrant testing confirms the excavation is clean before welding starts, and again after the repair weld is finished. On corrosion-resistant alloys this loop matters because a missed fragment of a crack can propagate through new weld metal. The report ties each repair to the original indication, with the excavation depth recorded where the operator's repair procedure requires it, so the history of the joint stays traceable. Heat-affected zones next to a repair are included in the examined area, since cracks often sit at the fusion line.

Sealing and machined surfaces at supply bases

At shore bases and shops, penetrant testing also examines equipment coming back from the field: valve bodies, flanges, hubs, wellhead and tree components, and machined seal surfaces. A crack-like flaw on a sealing face or in a corroded transition zone can leak under pressure, so these parts are checked after cleaning and before reuse. Highly polished or coated sealing faces need a penetrant system that does not attack the finish, and the procedure names it. The same approach applies to castings and forgings received before machining, where surface laps and shrink cracks are easiest to catch.

What the PT report contains

  • Platform or yard, component and weld ID, drawing reference, material and location
  • Procedure number and revision, the code and the acceptance criteria
  • Penetrant, remover and developer type with batch numbers, plus halogen and sulfur certification for corrosion-resistant alloys
  • Surface temperature, cleaning method, dwell and developing times
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, and the reviewing Level III
  • Indications with sketch or photograph, size and type, and accept or reject against the named criteria

What to send for an offshore PT quote

  • Platform location or yard address, and whether the work is offshore or onshore
  • Weld list or drawings, with material, diameter, thickness and number of joints
  • Code, specification and acceptance criteria
  • Requirements for halogen and sulfur certification of penetrant materials
  • Surface condition, coating status, access method and who prepares the surface
  • The operator's transport, safety training and permit requirements

Offshore logistics and planning

Transport, bed space and training requirements are set by the operator. Safety training such as offshore survival or helicopter egress may be needed depending on the platform and the transport mode, and we confirm and arrange it with the operator at the quote stage rather than claiming it up front. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, onshore or offshore. Weather affects both flights and the work itself, since wind, rain and high humidity interrupt penetrant application, so we plan float days and a sheltered work area. At fabrication yards, PT is sequenced after fit-up and grinding and before coating, hydrotest or load-out.

Where we work in the US for offshore

  • Houston: operator and engineering offices, and the many shops that fabricate alloy piping and skids for platforms.
  • New Orleans: Louisiana's offshore operations hub and its supply-base network on the Gulf coast.
  • Mobile: Alabama shipyards and fabricators building aluminum and steel marine structures.
  • Lake Charles: Calcasieu corridor yards with repair and heavy fabrication capability.
  • Corpus Christi: Texas coastal yards and the port serving Gulf energy projects.
  • Pascagoula: Mississippi marine fabrication and the shipbuilding base on the Gulf.

Training your own PT technicians

Companies that want their own penetrant technicians can study PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training and practice on the penetrant testing simulator, with the oil and gas NDT training page as the industry route. The employer certifies under its own written practice. For national background, see liquid penetrant testing services and the MT versus PT comparison.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools and does not offer underwater inspection or specialist techniques outside PT, MT and UT. We do not decide whether a flaw is acceptable for service or calculate remaining life; the operator's engineer makes those calls using our report.

faq.q: When should penetrant testing be used offshore instead of MT?
faq.a: Use PT on nonmagnetic metals such as stainless, duplex, nickel alloys and aluminum, or where magnetizing is impractical. MT remains faster and more sensitive on carbon steel structure and lifting gear.
No. Penetrant testing finds only flaws that are open to the surface. Internal flaws and wall loss need ultrasonic testing or another volumetric method, and many offshore programs pair the two.

faq.q: How do you keep salt from causing false indications?
faq.a: We remove the salt film and marine growth during precleaning, dry the surface fully, and shelter the work from spray. Doubtful indications are recleaned and retested before they are reported.

faq.q: Are penetrant materials controlled for corrosion-resistant alloys?
faq.a: Yes. ASME Section V Article 6 requires controlled halogen and sulfur content when testing austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys, and we retain and report the batch certifications for your quality file.

faq.q: Which codes govern offshore PT work in the US?
faq.a: BSEE 30 CFR Part 250 regulates Gulf operations, API RP 2A guides platform integrity, AWS D1.1 covers structural welds and ASME B31.3 covers piping. The method itself comes from ASME Section V Article 6, with ASTM E165 as common practice.
Yes, with penetrant testing. Aluminum is nonmagnetic, so PT of welds and fittings is the surface method. The operator or the helideck owner sets the acceptance criteria.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects penetrant indications?
faq.a: Our Level II technician evaluates and reports indications against the named criteria. The operator's inspector or engineer decides acceptance and repair, and an ASNT Level III approves our procedure.

faq.q: What safety training do your technicians need for offshore platforms?
faq.a: The operator sets it and it may include offshore survival or helicopter egress training. We confirm the requirement during quoting and arrange it with the operator instead of assuming we hold it.

faq.q: What do you need to quote an offshore PT job?
faq.a: The platform or yard location, a weld list or drawings, materials, code and acceptance criteria, halogen and sulfur certification needs, surface condition, access method and the operator's transport and permit requirements.
